The Claude reports were the simpler ones, and rework time wasn't counted
The pilot ran for six weeks rather than eight, so the sample is small
The manual reports were written by more junior staff than the Claude ones
explanation: Easier tasks in the Claude group plus uncounted rework inflate the speed gain, which undermines the comparison most directly. The other issues weaken it less.

question: A colleague asks Claude to build an automatic integration between the CRM and the billing system using custom code. What is the appropriate step for an associate?
options: Ask Claude to write and test the integration code, then hand it to IT to deploy
Route it to the technical team, describing the business need and required checks
Ask Claude to explain the integration options, then pick one and start building
Build a prototype in a test account first, then share it with the technical team
explanation: Custom integrations between business systems belong with the technical team. The associate's role is to describe the need and checks clearly. Writing or prototyping the code themselves goes beyond that role.

question: Before redesigning a slow purchase-approval process with Claude's help, what should the team do FIRST?
options: Ask Claude to draft a faster process based on industry best practice
Map the current process and measure where time is lost
Interview approvers about what they would change in the process
Automate the slowest approval step first, since it is the bottleneck
explanation: You need to see and measure the current process before redesigning it. Best practice and interviews help, but without measurement you may fix the wrong step. Naming a bottleneck before measuring is a guess.

question: In a meeting-notes workflow, Claude drafts the summary and an analyst checks it. Who should have the final check before distribution?
options: Claude, after a self-check prompt that asks it to verify accuracy
The analyst, who reviews it for accuracy and owns what is sent
The meeting chair, who should approve all summaries before release
The attendees, who can each correct their own parts after it is sent
explanation: The person who checks the summary owns what is sent. Claude's self-check isn't accountable review. Adding the chair may help, but the analyst is the defined final check, and correcting after sending is too late.

question: Which TWO practices make a pilot result convincing to sceptical stakeholders? (Select TWO.)
options: Measured results against a baseline, including time, quality and errors
A clear account of limitations and how they were handled
Detailed testimonials from users across every team in the pilot
A demonstration of the best outputs from the pilot period
Results from the strongest metrics, with a note that others are available
explanation: Measured results against a baseline and honest limitations build credibility. Testimonials and best-case demos are selective. Highlighting only the strongest metrics invites distrust.

question: A client uses many specialist abbreviations. How should an associate set up their client Project so Claude understands them?
options: Add the abbreviations to the associate's account-wide profile preferences
Put a glossary in the client's Project knowledge, plus an instruction to use it
Add the glossary to the Project knowledge without any extra instruction
Explain the abbreviations at the start of each chat in the Project
explanation: Client-specific context belongs in that client's Project, and an instruction makes sure Claude uses it. Profile preferences apply to every chat. A glossary without an instruction may be missed. Per-chat explanations are fragile.

question: How can a team stop a Project's policy knowledge from silently going stale?
options: Upload new versions whenever someone notices a change in the policy
Assign an owner to review on a set schedule, and keep a change log
Ask Claude to flag files that look outdated at the start of each chat
Add the date to each file name so users can see how old it is
explanation: An owner, a schedule and a change log stop knowledge going stale. Ad hoc updates, Claude's guesses and dated names all rely on someone noticing.

question: An associate set up several connectors months ago but now uses only one. What is the BEST practice?
options: Leave them connected, but tell Claude in each Project which one to use
Disconnect unused connectors to reduce unnecessary access
Leave them connected, since unused connectors don't access any data
Review them once a year and disconnect any that look unnecessary
explanation: Least privilege means removing access that isn't needed now. Instructions don't limit access. Waiting for an annual review leaves unneeded access in place in the meantime.

question: A Project's owner replaces the pricing file in its knowledge. What else should they do?
options: Ask Claude to confirm it has read the new file before users rely on it
Tell the Project's users what changed and when it takes effect
Start a new chat to make sure Claude uses the new file going forward
Keep the old file too, so users can compare the two price lists
explanation: Users need to know what changed and when. Asking Claude or starting a new chat doesn't inform anyone. Keeping the old file risks Claude quoting outdated prices.

question: A team's shared Project will contain a file with salary data that only managers should see. What is the BEST approach?
options: Upload it with an instruction telling Claude to share salary data only with managers
Keep it out of the shared Project, or use a separate Project only managers can access
Upload it to the shared Project, but only after removing employees' names
Upload it with a note asking non-managers not to ask about salaries
explanation: Access should be controlled by who can see the Project, not by instructions or requests. Removing names may not be enough, since roles and teams can identify people.

question: A status report must reflect a shared spreadsheet that changes several times a day. Which is the BEST setup?
options: Upload a fresh copy of the spreadsheet each morning before writing the report
Use an approved connector so Claude reads the live spreadsheet
Paste the latest figures into the chat each time the report is written
Upload a copy once a week and note the date it was taken in the report
explanation: An approved connector reads live data, which is what a several-times-a-day spreadsheet needs. Daily uploads and pasting still go stale within hours and add manual effort.

question: A Project's instructions say “use the attached price list,” but the knowledge contains both the 2025 and 2026 lists. Sales reps report old prices. What is the BEST fix?
options: Add “use the most recent list” to the instructions, keeping both lists for reference
Remove the 2025 list from knowledge, and name the current file in the instructions
Rename the 2025 file “OLD_price_list” so Claude knows not to use it
Add a note at the top of the 2026 list saying it replaces the 2025 list
explanation: Removing the outdated list and naming the current file removes the ambiguity. Renaming, notes or a “most recent” rule leave the old prices available to be quoted.

question: Customer data was approved for use in analyzing service quality. A colleague now wants to use the same data with Claude to target marketing offers. What is the issue?
options: None, provided the data stays inside the approved Claude workspace
Approval for one purpose doesn't cover another. Check consent and policy
Only that the marketing team needs separate access to the workspace
None, provided names are removed before the marketing analysis
explanation: Purpose limitation means approval is tied to a purpose. A new use needs its own check against policy and consent. Staying in the workspace or removing names doesn't settle whether the new purpose is allowed.

question: An associate thinks using an incognito or temporary chat makes it acceptable to paste regulated customer data into Claude. Is this correct?
options: Yes, because temporary chats aren't used to train models, which removes the main risk
No. It depends on policy and the approved workspace, not on the chat mode
Yes, if the data is limited to what the task needs and deleted afterwards
No. Regulated data can never be used with Claude under any circumstances
explanation: Chat mode doesn't change data obligations. Policy and the approved workspace decide what's allowed. Training use is only one consideration, and approved workspaces can permit regulated data where policy allows.

question: A consultant used Claude to prepare a deliverable for a client. What should they check before delivering it?
options: The firm's AI policy only, since the firm is responsible for the deliverable
The firm's AI policy and the client's terms on AI use, including disclosure
The client's terms only, since they are the ones receiving the work
Whether the deliverable passes an AI-detection tool before sending it
explanation: Both the firm's policy and the client's terms apply, including any disclosure requirements. AI-detection tools don't settle compliance.

question: An AI tool is set up to take actions on its own, such as deleting records or sending payments. What control is MOST important?
options: Detailed logging of every action so mistakes can be traced afterwards
Human approval before irreversible or high-impact actions
Clear written instructions describing which actions are allowed
A daily review of actions taken in the previous 24 hours
explanation: Approval before irreversible or high-impact actions prevents harm. Logging and daily reviews only catch problems after they happen. Instructions don't enforce limits.

question: The company-approved Claude workspace is slower to access than a personal account. An associate has an urgent deadline. What should they do?
options: Use the personal account this once, then redo the work in the approved one
Use the approved workspace, since policy still applies under time pressure
Use the personal account, but avoid pasting any confidential information
Ask their manager for permission to use the personal account this time
explanation: Policy applies under deadlines too. Avoiding confidential data still breaks the rule, and a manager can't approve a personal-account exception to company policy.

question: Which use of Claude in recruitment is LEAST appropriate?
options: Drafting rejection emails that recruiters personalize and send themselves
Summarizing interview notes for the panel to discuss together
Rejecting applicants automatically on Claude's screening, with no human review
Ranking applications for recruiters, who then review every candidate
explanation: Automated rejection with no human review is the least appropriate, because it makes consequential decisions about people without oversight. The others keep a person in charge of each decision.

question: How should the level of human review for Claude outputs be decided?
options: By the tool used, since outputs from more capable models need lighter review
In proportion to risk: light for low-stakes drafts, thorough for external or high-impact
By the author's experience, since senior staff need less review of their outputs
The same thorough level for every output, since any output could contain errors
explanation: Review should scale with the stakes. Uniform heavy review wastes effort on trivial drafts. Model tier or author seniority doesn't change the risk of the content.

question: Which statement about how Claude generates text is MOST accurate?
options: It retrieves the most relevant passages from its training data and combines them
It predicts likely text from learned patterns, so it can be fluent but wrong
It reasons step by step from facts it has verified, then writes the answer
It predicts likely text, and flags low-confidence statements automatically
explanation: Claude generates text by predicting likely continuations from learned patterns. That is why it can be fluent and still wrong. It doesn't retrieve or verify facts by default, or automatically flag uncertainty.

question: An associate wants to use customer survey responses with Claude. Which TWO steps BEST reflect consent and data-minimization principles? (Select TWO.)
options: Confirm the survey's consent terms cover this kind of analysis
Remove names and contact details not needed for the analysis
Keep names but remove email addresses, since names alone aren't sensitive
Check consent after the analysis, before sharing any results
Add purchase history to make the analysis more useful for the business
explanation: Confirming consent covers the purpose, and removing unneeded identifiers, reflect consent and minimization. Names are still personal data. Checking consent after the use is too late. Adding data goes against minimization.

question: A one-line prompt, “Sort these tickets,” gives inconsistent results. What is the BEST fix?
options: Add “sort them carefully and consistently” to the end of the prompt
Specify the categories, the criteria for each, and the output format
List the categories to sort into, and leave the criteria to Claude
Ask Claude to explain how it sorted them, then correct the mistakes
explanation: Consistent sorting needs defined categories, criteria and format. Categories without criteria still leave Claude guessing at the boundaries. Correcting after the fact doesn't stop inconsistency.

question: A Project assistant should say when its source documents don't cover a question, but it guesses instead. What should the associate change and test?
options: Add an instruction to say when sources don't cover it, and test with typical questions
Add an instruction to say when sources don't cover it, and test with out-of-scope questions
Upload more documents so the sources cover more questions, then test with typical ones
Ask users to check answers against the sources, so guesses are caught afterwards
explanation: The fix is an explicit instruction, and the test must use questions the sources deliberately don't cover. Testing with typical questions won't show whether the new behavior works.

question: A format rule is buried in paragraph six of a long prompt, and Claude ignores it. What is the BEST fix?
options: Move the format rule to the first paragraph, and keep the rest of the prompt as it is
Move format rules into a short list near the end of the request, with an example
Repeat the format rule in capital letters in paragraph six so it stands out
Keep the rule in paragraph six and ask Claude to read the whole prompt carefully
explanation: A short, clear list near the end, with an example of the output, makes format rules easy to follow. Moving one rule to the top helps a little, but without an example it can still be missed. Capitals and pleas are weak fixes.

question: Meeting summaries from a Project keep missing action owners. What is the BEST way to fix this and confirm the fix?
options: Add “include action owners” to the instructions, and check the next meeting's summary
Require owners in the Project instructions, then test on several past meetings
Ask Claude in each chat to list the action owners at the end of the summary
Add a template with an owners column, and trust that Claude will fill it in
explanation: Change the instructions, then test on several past meetings to confirm the fix works across cases. Checking one future meeting is a thin test, and per-chat asks or an untested template don't confirm anything.

question: In a very long chat, Claude's answers start contradicting earlier decisions. What is this commonly called, and how is it fixed?
options: Context overflow. Delete the earliest messages so the latest decisions take priority
Context drift, or context rot. Summarize the agreed decisions and continue in a fresh chat
Hallucination. Ask Claude to check its answers against the earlier decisions
Context drift. Restate every earlier decision in each new message in the same chat
explanation: This is context drift (context rot). Summarizing agreed decisions and continuing fresh is the reliable fix. Restating everything in the same chat keeps adding to the bloat, and deleting messages can lose decisions.

question: An associate's report prompt asks Claude to “be more detailed” each time the output is too thin, but quality doesn't improve. What is the MOST effective change?
options: Specify a minimum length for each section, such as at least 300 words
Break the report into stages and specify what each section must cover
Provide a longer example report and ask Claude to match its level of detail
Ask Claude to list what is missing from the thin draft, then add it
explanation: Staging the work and defining required content per section addresses the cause. Length minimums add padding. An example helps with style, but not with what this report must cover. Claude's own gap list doesn't know what the reader needs.

question: An associate's prompt reads: “Write something about our return policy.” The draft is generic. Which rewrite fixes the MOST important gaps?
options: “Write a detailed, professional piece about our return policy for customers, covering every rule so nothing is left out.”
“For first-time online customers: explain our 30-day return policy in a friendly tone, in five short bullets.”
“You are a customer-service expert. Write about our return policy in a way customers will appreciate.”
“Write about our return policy, and make it clear, accurate and engaging for anyone who reads it.”
explanation: The second rewrite adds audience, purpose, tone, length and format. The others add adjectives or a role but still leave the audience and output shape for Claude to guess.

question: Which order of prompt parts usually reads MOST naturally to Claude for a business request?
options: Task first, then context, then constraints, then format, so Claude knows the goal before the background
Context, then task, then format and constraints, so the request builds from situation to output
Format first, then task, then context, so Claude knows the output shape before reading anything else
Constraints first, then context, then task, so the limits frame everything that follows them
explanation: Context, then task, then format and constraints mirrors how you'd brief a colleague: the situation, what you need, and the shape and limits. Order isn't a hard rule, but this one keeps requests easy to follow.

question: A support lead wants every complaint reply drafted in the same warm, apologetic voice. Which combination of techniques gives the MOST consistent result?
options: A role (“experienced, empathetic support agent”) plus one or two real replies that show the voice
A role (“experienced, empathetic support agent”) plus a list of adjectives describing the voice
A detailed paragraph describing the voice, plus an instruction to keep it the same every time
Two real example replies, plus an instruction to vary the wording so replies don't sound templated
explanation: A role sets the overall stance, and real examples show the exact voice. Adjectives and descriptions are harder for Claude to match. Asking for variation works against the consistency the lead wants.

question: A prompt gives Claude a role and rich background, but the output is still not usable. Rereading it, the associate sees it never says what to produce. What is the BEST next step?
options: Add more background, since a richer picture of the situation usually fixes unusable output
State the task and the output format explicitly, then compare the new result with the old one
Switch the role to a more senior expert, since a stronger persona produces more usable work
Ask Claude what it thinks the associate wants, then accept whatever deliverable it suggests
explanation: The missing ingredient is the task and the format. Adding background or changing the role doesn't tell Claude what to deliver. Letting Claude choose the deliverable gives up control of the result.

question: An associate asks Claude to “give me feedback on this proposal” and gets a page of general comments. Which revision would help MOST?
options: “Give me detailed, honest feedback on this proposal, and don't hold back on any criticism.”
“Give feedback on structure and clarity for a CFO audience, as the top five issues ranked.”
“Give me feedback on this proposal, covering all aspects, so I can improve it before sending.”
“Act as a senior consultant and give me thorough feedback on this proposal before I send it.”
explanation: Naming the kind of feedback, the audience and a ranked, limited format focuses the review. “Honest”, “all aspects” or a consultant role still leave Claude to decide what matters.

question: A request has clear context, task and format, but no length guidance, and Claude's reply is three times longer than needed. Which change is MOST precise?
options: Add “be concise” at the end, so Claude knows that length matters for this request
Add a specific limit, such as “in three sentences” or “under 80 words”
Remove some of the context, since a long prompt tends to produce a long reply
Ask Claude to shorten the reply afterwards, repeating until it reaches the right size
explanation: A measurable limit is the most precise fix. “Be concise” is vague, cutting useful context risks worse output, and repeated shortening takes extra rounds.

question: A first draft from Claude has the right content but the wrong tone for the audience. What does a good iteration loop suggest doing next?
options: Rewrite the whole prompt from scratch, since the first version clearly didn't work
Name the audience and the tone you want, and keep the rest of the prompt unchanged
Ask Claude to try again with no changes, since a second attempt often fixes the tone
Add a role and an example, change the format, and tighten the length all at once
explanation: Iteration means reading the result, spotting what's wrong, and making a targeted change. Rewriting everything or changing many things at once makes it hard to know what helped, and an unchanged retry may repeat the problem.

question: A prompt reads: “Fix this email, write a LinkedIn post about the launch, and plan next week's team agenda.” The results are shallow. What is the BEST first step?
options: Add audience and tone details to the single prompt, so all three outputs improve together in one pass
Split it into three separate prompts, then add audience, tone and format details to each one
Number the three tasks in the same prompt, so Claude gives each one its own section
Ask for the three tasks to be done in more depth, keeping them together for efficiency
explanation: Unrelated tasks bundled together get shallow treatment. Splitting them, then specifying each one, fixes both problems. Numbering or asking for depth keeps the bundle.

question: A colleague says: “Claude sounded completely sure, so the figure must be right.” What is the MOST accurate response?
options: Claude's tone does reflect its certainty, so a confident, specific answer is a reasonable signal it's correct
Tone isn't evidence. Claude can state wrong facts just as fluently as right ones, so check key figures
Confident answers are usually right, so only figures that sound hesitant need to be checked
Ask Claude whether it is sure, and accept the figure if it confirms it a second time
explanation: Fluency and confidence don't indicate accuracy. Important figures need checking against a trusted source. Asking Claude to confirm itself isn't verification.

question: Which kind of content in a Claude draft carries the HIGHEST risk of a confident error?
options: General explanations of well-known concepts, written for a non-specialist audience
Specific numbers, names, dates, quotes and anything about recent events
Rewordings of text the associate pasted into the chat, kept close to the original
Lists of brainstormed ideas, where many options are deliberately speculative
explanation: Specific facts such as numbers, names, dates and quotes, and recent events, are where hallucinations most often appear and matter most. Brainstorms are meant to be speculative, and rewording supplied text is lower risk.

question: A procurement officer asks Claude for a competitor's “current” price without supplying any recent data. What is the MAIN risk?
options: Claude will refuse, because pricing information is commercially sensitive
The answer may come from older training data and be out of date, even if it sounds current
Claude will search the competitor's website automatically, which may breach that site's terms of use
The price may be in a different currency, so it will need converting before use
explanation: Without supplied data or a search tool, Claude answers from training data that has a cutoff. The figure may be stale even when it's stated confidently.

question: What does a model's knowledge cutoff mean for a business user?
options: Claude stops answering questions about topics it learned about before that date
Claude's built-in knowledge ends at that date, so later events need to be supplied or searched
Claude can recall anything up to that date perfectly, so only later facts need checking
Claude's memory of earlier chats is deleted at that date, so older conversations can't be continued
explanation: The cutoff is when training data was collected. Claude can still be wrong about earlier facts, so checking still matters. Newer information has to be provided, or found with search.

question: A team needs Claude's help with a briefing on a regulation that changed last month. Which approach is MOST reliable?
options: Ask Claude to explain the regulation, and add a note that it may be slightly out of date
Give Claude the current text or use search with citations, then check key points against the source
Ask Claude what it knows about recent changes, and use only the parts it says it's fully confident about
Use Claude's explanation of the old rules, since most regulations change only in minor ways
explanation: Recent changes may be past the knowledge cutoff. Supplying the current text, or using search with citations, then checking against the source, is reliable. A caveat or Claude's self-reported confidence doesn't fix stale content.

question: A financial analyst isn't sure about one statistic Claude included in a client report. What is the BEST practice?
options: Ask Claude where the statistic came from, and keep it if Claude names a credible source
Check the statistic against a trusted primary source before it goes into the report
Round the statistic so that a small error won't matter in the final report
Keep it, but add a footnote saying figures were produced with AI assistance
explanation: Check specific figures against a trusted source before use. Claude can name sources that don't exist or don't support the figure. Rounding or a footnote doesn't make a wrong figure right.

question: Why does verifying one key number in a Claude draft often take only a few minutes?
options: Because Claude marks the numbers it is unsure about, so you know exactly which ones to check
Because checking one specific fact against a source is quick, unlike re-checking the whole draft
Because numbers in Claude drafts are usually correct, so a quick look is normally enough
Because a second AI tool can confirm the number instantly, without needing to find the original source
explanation: Targeted checks of specific facts are fast and catch the errors that matter. Claude doesn't reliably flag its own uncertainty, and another AI tool isn't a primary source.

question: Which approach to reviewing Claude's answers is MOST efficient and safe?
options: Apply the same thorough review to every answer, so nothing important slips through
Scale scrutiny to the stakes: light for routine drafts, careful checks for facts and high-impact uses
Review only answers that look wrong or surprising, since most answers are correct and checking wastes time
Review answers on topics Claude is weaker at, and trust those on topics it knows well
explanation: Scrutiny should scale with the stakes. Uniform review wastes time on low-stakes drafts. Reviewing only what looks wrong misses confident errors, and you can't reliably tell which topics Claude knows well.

question: A colleague asks Claude for yesterday's match result and tomorrow's exact temperature, without search turned on. What should they expect?
options: Both answers will be accurate, because Claude has access to live sports and weather data by default
Neither can be relied on: the match is past the cutoff, and the forecast needs live data
The match result will be accurate, but the temperature will be an estimate
Claude will refuse both questions, since it can't discuss events or the weather
explanation: Without search or supplied data, Claude has no reliable access to recent events or live forecasts. It may still produce an answer, which is why such answers need checking.

question: A request reads: “What was our exact revenue last quarter, to the dollar?” Why does this need extra care?
options: Because Claude can't do arithmetic, so it will refuse to give a figure
It's a specific, high-stakes number, so take it from the finance system or verify it there
Because revenue is confidential, so Claude will give only a rounded estimate
Because questions about exact money figures need the most capable model tier to answer accurately
explanation: Exact financial figures are high-stakes and specific, so the reliable source is the company's own finance system. A capable model can still misstate a figure it was never given.

question: An associate uses Claude to draft a reply to a hospital patient's question about medication timing. What is the MOST appropriate review?
options: Check the tone is warm and the reply is easy to understand, then send it
Have a qualified clinician check the medical content before anything is sent to the patient
Ask Claude to add a disclaimer that it is not medical advice, then send it
Compare it with a similar reply sent to another patient last month, and send it if the advice matches
explanation: Medical guidance to patients is high-stakes, so a qualified person must check the content. A disclaimer or a past reply doesn't make the advice correct for this patient.

question: A comms team traces a Claude-drafted statistic back to its original source before a public announcement. What does this show?
options: Unnecessary caution, since Claude's statistics are reliable enough for public use
Output verification matched to the stakes of a public, attributable statement
A lack of trust in Claude, which slows down the team's announcement process
Good practice only if the statistic looked unusual or surprising to the team
explanation: Public statements carry reputational risk, so checking statistics against the original source is proportionate. A plausible-looking figure needs checking too, since errors don't always look unusual.

question: In a set of Claude-drafted customer replies, which TWO findings MOST clearly mean a reply must be fixed before sending? (Select TWO.)
options: A refund amount that doesn't match the order record
A promised delivery date the business never agreed
A greeting that is slightly more formal than usual
A reply that is two sentences longer than the template
A sentence that could be split into two for readability
explanation: A wrong amount and an unagreed commitment are factual errors that could cost money and trust. Formality, length and sentence structure are style points that may be worth adjusting, but don't make a reply wrong.

question: An associate is tired of re-explaining their role, team and writing preferences in every new chat. Which feature is designed for this, and what is the main caution?
options: Memory, which carries details across chats. Review what it stores and keep sensitive data out
Chat history, so Claude reads all earlier conversations automatically before answering each new message
A Project for each topic, since Projects are the only way to keep any details between separate chats
Memory, which should be filled with as much personal and client detail as possible so answers are fully tailored
explanation: Memory carries useful context between chats. The caution is to review and edit what it holds, and to follow policy on sensitive data. Chat history lets you find past chats, but they aren't all read automatically. Projects help, but they aren't the only option, and filling memory with client data creates risk.

question: An associate wants a reusable one-page checklist tool that colleagues can open, tick through and share. Which output fits BEST?
options: An inline chat answer formatted as a bulleted list, which colleagues can copy from the conversation
An artifact, since it's substantial, standalone content meant to be reused, edited and shared
A Project knowledge file, so the checklist is available whenever anyone asks about it in chat
A long answer split across several messages, so each section of the checklist can be reviewed separately
explanation: Artifacts suit substantial, standalone content you'll reuse, edit or share, such as documents and interactive tools. A list in chat is fine for quick answers, but it isn't a usable tool. A knowledge file is reference material, not something colleagues tick through.

question: A legal operations lead needs Claude to cross-check 30 long supplier contracts for subtle conflicts between clauses. Speed is not a concern. Which model choice fits BEST?
options: The fastest, lightest tier, since the contracts are already written and only need comparing
The most capable tier, since subtle cross-document reasoning matters more than speed here
Whichever tier is set as the default, since tier choice mainly affects response speed
A balanced tier for half the contracts and the lightest tier for the rest, to keep costs even
explanation: Subtle reasoning across many long documents is where the most capable tier earns its extra time and cost. Tiers differ in reasoning ability, not just speed, and splitting tiers arbitrarily makes the results uneven.

question: An associate needs today's exchange rate for one currency pair, and separately a cited, multi-source report on supply-chain regulation. Which choice of features is BEST?
options: Research for both, since it is the most thorough way to get any current information with sources
Web search for the quick rate, and Research for the multi-source report with citations
Claude's built-in knowledge for the rate, and web search for the report, one query at a time
Extended thinking for both, since careful reasoning improves accuracy for financial and regulatory topics
explanation: A single current fact suits a quick web search. A report drawing on many sources suits Research, which gathers and cites more widely. Built-in knowledge can't give today's rate, and extended thinking doesn't fetch new information.

question: An associate photographs a whiteboard full of handwritten workshop notes and wants them as a tidy action list. What is the BEST approach?
options: Retype the notes by hand first, since Claude can't read text from photos or images
Upload the photo, ask Claude to transcribe and organize it, then check the result against the board
Upload the photo and turn on extended thinking, since that guarantees an accurate transcription
Upload the photo and send the list straight to attendees, since transcription errors from photos are rare
explanation: Claude can read images, so upload the photo and have it transcribe and organize the notes. Handwriting can be misread, so check the result before sharing. Extended thinking doesn't guarantee accuracy, and skipping the check risks wrong owners or dates.

question: Staff will use a simple internal helper hundreds of times a day to look up short answers from a clear policy FAQ. Which model choice is MOST sensible?
options: The most capable tier, since staff will rely on the answers and accuracy always comes first
A fast, light tier, checked on a sample of real questions to confirm the answers meet the bar
A fast, light tier with no testing, since FAQ lookups are always simple enough for any model
Extended thinking on every request, so each short lookup gets the most careful answer possible
explanation: High-volume, simple lookups suit a fast, low-cost tier, as long as a sample of real questions confirms it meets the quality bar. Skipping the test is the weak point in the third option. The most capable tier or extended thinking adds cost and delay the task doesn't need.

question: Two associates use different Claude tiers for tasks that look similar: tagging support tickets and drafting a sensitive complaint reply. Which explanation is MOST accurate?
options: One of them is wrong, since similar-looking tasks should always use the same tier
The needs differ: tagging is high-volume and simple, the reply is high-stakes and nuanced
The most capable tier should be used for both, since quality always matters
The lightest tier should be used for both, since both are short pieces of text
explanation: Tier choice depends on what the task needs: speed and cost for simple high-volume work, depth for nuanced, high-stakes writing. Tasks that look alike can need different tiers.

question: A payroll team needs exact commission payouts for 1,200 employees from a detailed formula. What is the BEST use of tools?
options: Have Claude calculate all 1,200 payouts in chat, then spot-check a sample of results against the formula
Run it in a spreadsheet or payroll system, and use Claude to explain results or draft messages
Have Claude write the formula, then run it in chat on the full data set
Split the employees into batches of 100 and have Claude calculate each batch
explanation: Precise calculation at scale belongs in a dedicated system. Claude adds value around it, such as explaining results or drafting messages. Batching or spot-checking doesn't make chat-based arithmetic the right tool.

question: Which task is the WEAKEST fit for Claude on its own?
options: Summarizing 500 customer survey responses into themes
Tracking delivery trucks' live locations in real time
Explaining a technical concept for a non-technical audience
Brainstorming taglines for a new product launch
explanation: Live, real-time tracking needs a purpose-built system with live data feeds. The others are language and reasoning tasks Claude does well.

question: When deciding whether a new, unfamiliar task suits Claude, which set of questions is MOST useful?
options: Is it urgent? Is it new? Has anyone else on the team tried it with Claude before, and did it work?
Does it need language or reasoning? Live data? Exact maths at scale? What's at stake?
Is it long? Is it creative? Would the most capable model tier be needed?
Is it repetitive? Is it boring? Would automating it save the most time?
explanation: Asking about language and reasoning, live data, exact calculation and stakes points the task to Claude, another tool, or a mix. Urgency, length or tedium don't tell you whether Claude fits.

question: A team lead skips Claude for brainstorming packaging ideas, saying “it doesn't need a special tool.” What is the BEST response?
options: Agree, since brainstorming is quick and people come up with better ideas without tools
Point out that idea generation is a strong fit for Claude, and suggest trying it for a wider range
Agree, but suggest using Claude afterwards to check the ideas for spelling
Suggest using the most capable model tier, since creative tasks like this need the deepest reasoning available
explanation: Brainstorming is one of Claude's strengths, and skipping it misses an easy win. Using Claude only for spelling undersells it, and a lighter or balanced tier is usually fine for ideation.

question: A team's task involves web research, organizing the numbers, and building slides, using several Claude surfaces. What is the MAIN risk to manage?
options: Using more than one surface, since doing everything in one place is always more reliable
Losing or changing a number or fact as information moves between surfaces
Running out of usage limits, since each surface has a separate allowance
Getting different writing styles from each surface, since they use different models
explanation: Moving between surfaces can suit each step, but facts and figures can be lost or altered in transfer, so check them at each handoff. Switching surfaces isn't a problem in itself.

question: A finance team is sorting tasks into automate, augment, or human-only. Which classification is MOST appropriate?
options: Approving a supplier's disputed invoice: automate, since the rules are written down in policy
Drafting variance commentary for the finance lead to edit: augment, with a human deciding
Deciding whether to dismiss an employee over expenses: augment, with Claude recommending the outcome
Formatting a routine internal report from approved figures: human-only, since figures are involved
explanation: Drafting for a person to edit and decide is classic augmentation. Disputed approvals need human judgment, so they can't be automated. Dismissal decisions are human-only. Routine formatting of approved figures is low-risk and a good candidate for automation with checks.

question: A sales manager re-explains the same three key accounts at the start of every chat. Which setup saves the MOST time over months?
options: One Project for all three accounts, with every account's files mixed together
A Project for each account, holding its background, files and instructions
A profile preference listing all three accounts' details for every chat
A saved document of the background to paste in at the start of each chat
explanation: A Project per account keeps each account's context separate and ready in every new chat. Mixing accounts risks confusion, profile preferences apply everywhere, and pasting still repeats the work.

question: A team chains prompts: extract figures from reports, analyze trends, draft a briefing, then publish. Where is a human checkpoint MOST valuable?
options: Only at the end, after publishing, so reviewers can see the briefing exactly as readers will
After extraction, to check the figures against the source before errors flow into later steps
Only before the analysis step, since that is where Claude is most likely to make reasoning errors
At no fixed point. Reviewers should dip in whenever they have time during the week
explanation: In a chain, early errors compound. Checking extracted figures before analysis stops wrong numbers from spreading. A check after publishing is too late, and ad hoc checks aren't a control. A final review before publishing is also wise, but the early check prevents the most downstream damage.

question: Which TWO tasks are BEST handed to Claude rather than a specialized system? (Select TWO.)
options: Summarizing themes from 500 open-ended survey comments
Drafting a plain-language explanation of a new policy
Calculating exact refund totals across 3,000 orders
Monitoring live stock levels across ten warehouses
Reconciling bank transactions to the cent each month
explanation: Summarizing text and explaining in plain language are core language tasks. Exact totals, live monitoring and reconciliation to the cent need dedicated systems with precise calculation or live data.

question: A retail team assigns every task on its list to Claude, including live inventory tracking. What is the MOST likely issue?
options: Nothing, since Claude can handle any business task if the prompt is clear enough
Live tracking needs a purpose-built system with live data, so that task belongs elsewhere
The tasks should be split across several model tiers instead of one
The team should use the most capable model tier for all of them, since inventory and most other tasks are numerical
explanation: Claude complements other tools. Live tracking needs real-time data feeds, which a chat assistant doesn't have by default. Changing tiers or surfaces doesn't solve that.

question: A consultant always wants concise, no-fluff answers in every conversation. What is the MOST efficient setup?
options: Add “be concise” to the custom instructions of each Project they use
Set the preference once in profile settings, so it applies across conversations
Start every new chat with a short message asking for concise answers
Create a Project called “Concise” with that instruction, and hold all conversations inside it
explanation: Profile preferences apply across all conversations, so the rule is set once. Per-Project or per-chat instructions repeat the work, and one catch-all Project mixes unrelated work.

question: An HR specialist is drafting a handbook section as an artifact and asks for a warmer tone. What happens?
options: Claude writes a new version in the chat, which then has to be pasted over the old one
The artifact updates in its own panel, so the content stays in one place
A new Project is created to hold the revised version separately
The tone change applies to future artifacts only, not the current one
explanation: Artifacts show content in a separate panel that updates in place as you ask for changes, so you don't need to copy and paste between versions.

question: A project lead returns from leave and wants the draft plan she discussed with Claude a week ago. What is the BEST approach?
options: Ask Claude in a new chat to recall last week's plan, since it remembers earlier chats
Search chat history for the conversation and continue it there
Start the plan again from scratch, since old chats can't be reopened
Ask a colleague to forward their copy of the plan from their own chats
explanation: Chat history lets you find and continue earlier conversations. A new chat won't automatically recall a separate conversation unless memory features are set up and enabled.

question: Claude, connected to the team's shared drive, keeps quoting an outdated version of the travel policy. Two versions sit in different folders. What is the BEST fix?
options: Tell Claude in each chat to ignore the older file, since a connector's file access can't be adjusted
Archive or remove the outdated version, and point Claude to the current file's location
Disconnect the drive and paste the policy into every chat that needs it
Rename the current file “FINAL” so Claude recognizes it as the right version
explanation: Claude reads what the connector gives it access to, so conflicting versions cause conflicting answers. Removing the outdated copy and naming the current source fixes the cause. Per-chat reminders and “FINAL” names are fragile, and dropping the connector loses its benefit.

question: A Project holds 60 long knowledge files. Claude often misses a key clause buried in one of them, though it finds it when that file is attached alone. What is the BEST improvement?
options: Upload the file a second time, so the clause appears twice in the Project's knowledge
Trim the knowledge to what the Project needs, and name the specific document when asking
Ask Claude to read every file more carefully before answering any question in the Project
Move all 60 files into one combined PDF, so Claude has a single document to search through
explanation: Large amounts of loosely relevant material make specific details easier to miss. Curating the knowledge, and pointing Claude to the right document, improves recall. Duplicates add noise, “read carefully” changes nothing, and one giant PDF makes the problem worse.

question: What is a token, in the context of Claude?
options: One full word, so token counts always match word counts exactly
A small chunk of text, often part of a word, that Claude reads and writes
One sentence, which is the unit used to measure Claude's usage limits and costs
A login credential that allows an app to connect to Claude
explanation: Tokens are small pieces of text, often parts of words. That's why token counts don't match word counts exactly, and why longer inputs and outputs use more of a limit or budget.

question: After hours of pasting new documents into one chat, Claude warns that the conversation is getting too long. What is the BEST next step?
options: Keep going and paste shorter excerpts, since the warning only matters for very large files
Ask Claude for a summary of decisions so far, then continue in a new chat with that summary
Delete earlier messages one by one until the warning disappears, then carry on as before
Switch to a lighter model tier, since lighter tiers can hold much longer conversations and more documents
explanation: The context window holds the whole conversation, including every pasted document. Summarizing and continuing fresh keeps the decisions and frees space. Documents used repeatedly belong in Project knowledge rather than being pasted again. Tier choice doesn't fix an overfull conversation.

question: An employee is about to paste a customer's full account number into a general chat to get help drafting a reply. What is the BEST practice?
options: Paste it, since the chat is private and only the employee can see it
Mask or remove the number unless it's needed and policy allows it in this tool
Paste only the last eight digits, which is usually enough to protect the customer
Paste it, then delete the chat once the reply is finished
explanation: If the account number isn't needed for the task, mask or remove it, and follow policy on what the tool may hold. Partial numbers can still identify accounts, and deleting the chat afterwards doesn't undo sharing.

question: Which of these is the FIRST data-handling question an associate should be able to answer before using Claude at work?
options: Which model tier the company has approved for confidential client work
What company policy says may be shared with AI tools
Whether their chats are saved in chat history
How many tokens a typical document uses
explanation: Knowing the organization's policy on what data can go into AI tools comes first, because the rules differ between organizations. The other points are useful but don't decide what may be shared.

question: An HR coordinator drafting a reference letter replaces the employee's ID number and home address with placeholders before asking Claude for help. What principle is this?
options: Anonymization, which makes any HR document safe to share with any tool
Data minimization: sharing only what the task needs, masking the rest
Prompt injection defense, which stops Claude from leaking the details
Encryption, which protects the details while they're in the chat
explanation: Masking details the task doesn't need is data minimization. It reduces risk, but doesn't make every document safe for every tool, and it isn't encryption or an injection defense.

question: A request reads: “Summarize this customer's full account file, including their card number.” What is the MAIN concern?
options: The summary may be too long if the account file is large
It shares sensitive payment data that a summary doesn't need
Claude may refuse to summarize financial documents of any kind
The card number may be summarized incorrectly in the output
explanation: Card numbers are sensitive payment data, and a summary doesn't need them. They should be removed before sharing, whatever the length or accuracy of the summary.

question: A scheduling coordinator shares only the appointment type, not the patient's medical history, when asking Claude to draft a reminder. What does this show?
options: Unnecessary caution, since medical history improves the quality of the reminder
Sharing only what the task needs, consistent with responsible data handling
A misunderstanding, since health data is fine in any chat that isn't shared
Good practice only if the patient hasn't given consent to share their records
explanation: The reminder only needs the appointment type. Leaving out medical history follows data minimization whether or not consent exists, and health data needs particular care.

question: An associate thinks a temporary chat is fine for pasting full customer ID numbers “just this once.” Which response is MOST accurate?
options: Correct, since temporary chats aren't saved and so data obligations don't apply
Policy and the approved tool decide, not chat mode, so mask or leave the IDs out
Correct, as long as only a few IDs are pasted and the temporary chat is closed straight away afterwards
Incorrect only for health data. Other personal data is fine in temporary chats
explanation: Chat mode doesn't change what policy allows. If the IDs aren't needed, mask or leave them out. Volume or speed of deletion doesn't make sharing permitted.

question: Why does good data handling with Claude mostly need awareness rather than technical skill?
options: Because the AI tool detects and removes sensitive data automatically before processing it
Because habits like pausing before pasting and masking details are simple to follow
Because only IT teams are responsible for what data goes into AI tools
Because data rules are the same everywhere, so they're easy to memorize
explanation: Simple habits such as thinking before pasting, masking unnecessary details and checking policy prevent most problems. Tools don't strip sensitive data reliably, rules differ between organizations, and everyone shares responsibility.

question: An organization's AI data rules differ from those at an associate's previous employer. What should the associate do?
options: Follow the stricter of the two sets of rules, to be on the safe side
Learn and follow the current organization's policy, since rules vary between organizations
Follow the previous employer's rules until told otherwise, since they're already familiar and tested
Follow general best practice only, since company policies are usually out of date
explanation: Each organization sets its own rules, so the current employer's policy applies. Being stricter than policy is fine in places, but the policy defines what's allowed and what's required.

question: Before pasting a document into Claude, which TWO checks matter MOST? (Select TWO.)
options: Does it contain personal or sensitive details the task doesn't need?
Does company policy allow this kind of data in this tool?
Is the document short enough to fit in one message?
Was the document written by someone in the associate's own team?
Will the chat be saved in history after the task is done?
explanation: Removing details the task doesn't need, and confirming policy allows this data in this tool, are the key checks. Length, authorship and history settings don't decide whether sharing is appropriate.

question: An answer still feels generic even after the associate specified length and format. What is MOST likely missing?
options: A more capable model tier, since generic answers come from lighter tiers
The audience, purpose or context, which tell Claude who it's for and why
A stricter length limit, since shorter answers are less generic
Capital letters on the key instructions, so Claude pays closer attention
explanation: Length and format shape the output, but audience, purpose and context make it specific. A different tier, a tighter limit or capitals don't supply the missing information.

question: A request asks for “the pros and cons of switching vendors” and returns a dense paragraph that's hard to scan. What is the BEST fix?
options: Ask Claude to be clearer, since the content was hard to read
Ask for a table with Pros and Cons columns for each vendor
Ask for a shorter answer, so the paragraph is easier to scan
Ask Claude to rewrite the paragraph in simpler language
explanation: The missing piece is a requested format. A table with named columns makes a comparison easy to scan. Shorter or simpler prose is still a paragraph.

question: A team keeps getting Claude replies in paragraphs, though the person wants bullets in every chat. Their Projects say nothing about format. What should they check FIRST?
options: Whether the model tier supports bullet points in its replies
Whether the bullet preference is actually saved in their profile settings
Whether each Project needs its own instruction asking for bullets
Whether Claude has been told the preference enough times in past chats to remember it
explanation: A preference meant for every chat belongs in profile settings, so first confirm it's saved there. Corrections in past chats don't carry over, and all tiers can write bullets.

question: An associate keeps asking Claude to “improve” a draft, and each version changes in random ways. What is the MOST effective fix?
options: Keep asking, since the draft will settle into a good version after a few more rounds of improvement
Say exactly what to change, such as clarity of the opening or the length of section 2
Ask Claude to make only small improvements each time
Start a new chat for each round, so earlier versions don't interfere
explanation: Iteration works when each round targets a specific problem. “Improve” is undefined, so changes are random. Small or fresh-chat rounds still lack direction.

question: An associate's prompt to Claude reads only: “Is this a good idea?” and the reply is unhelpful. What is the BEST diagnosis?
options: The question is too short for Claude to process properly
There's no context: no idea described, no goal and no criteria for “good”
The question needs a role, such as “act as a business strategist”
The question should be asked in a Project with relevant files, rather than in a plain chat
explanation: Claude can't judge an idea it hasn't been given, against goals and criteria it doesn't know. A role or a Project doesn't fill in the missing context.

question: Claude's weekly status extracts feed a tracker, but the columns come back in a different order each week and break the import. Which change fixes this MOST reliably?
options: Ask Claude to “keep the same format as last week” at the start of each weekly request
Specify the exact column headers and order with a sample row, and check each output against it
Let Claude choose the clearest column order each week, then reorder the columns by hand
Switch to the most capable model tier, since it follows formatting instructions more consistently each week
explanation: A strict, explicit schema with an example, plus a quick check against it, makes output consistent. “Same as last week” relies on memory between chats. Reordering by hand wastes the time saved, and a stronger model still needs the schema stated.
